t: Encode String with Shortest Length — Interval DP with Repeat Detection
o: We must return the shortest encoding of `s` where any substring that is a repetition of a smaller block may be written as `k[block]`. Encoding can be nested (a block itself may be encoded), so this is naturally an interval problem: for every substring we need its best encoding, built from smaller substrings. With n ≤ 150 there are O(n²) substrings; checking whether a substring is periodic takes O(n) per candidate divisor, giving roughly O(n³·d(n)) overall — fast enough. The key trick for detecting that `t` is made of repeated copies of some block: if `t` appears as a proper prefix of `(t + t)[1:]`, then `t` is periodic, and the smallest such occurrence index gives the period.
k: Any optimal encoding of s decomposes into an encoded piece plus the optimal encodings of two subintervals, so interval DP over (i, j) works.
A string t is k-periodic iff t occurs in (t+t) starting at some index p < len(t); then t = t[:p] repeated len(t)/p times.
Only encode when it strictly shortens the string: compare len(k[...]) against the raw length before choosing.

a.i: Define solve(i, j) = shortest encoding of s[i..j]. Either split s[i..j] at every position into two independently-encoded halves, or detect that s[i..j] is a repetition of a shorter block and encode it as k[solve(block)]. Memoization on (i, j) keeps each state computed once. This mirrors how nested encodings like 2[2[a]b] arise naturally from recursion.
s: Precompute nothing; write a recursive function dp(i, j) returning the best encoding of s[i..j], memoized by (i, j).
Base case: single character returns that character.
Candidate 1: try every split point m in [i+1, j-1]; candidate = dp(i, m-1) + dp(m, j).
Candidate 2: find the smallest p such that s[i..j] equals s[i..i+p-1] repeated; if found, candidate = str(count) + '[' + dp(i, i+p-1) + ']'.
Return the shortest candidate among all options.
a.t: O(n^3 · d(n)) where d(n) is the number of divisors — O(n²) states, each doing O(n) splits plus O(n) periodicity check via string search.
a.sp: O(n³) total — O(n²) memo entries each storing strings up to length n.

a.i: Same recurrence as Approach 1 but iterated by increasing substring length, which avoids recursion overhead and hash-map lookups. We keep a 2-D table dp[i][j] holding the best encoding of s[i..j]. The periodicity test uses the classic doubling trick: t is periodic with period p iff (t+t).indexOf(t, 1) == p.
s: Create dp as an n×n table; initialize dp[i][i] = s[i].
For each length L from 2 to n, for each start i with j = i + L - 1:
Start with best = raw substring s[i..j].
Try all splits m: candidate dp[i][m-1] + dp[m][j]; keep the shortest.
Compute p = (t+t).indexOf(t, 1); if p < L, also consider str(L/p) + '[' + dp[i][i+p-1] + ']' when shorter; store result in dp[i][j] and return dp[0][n-1].
a.t: O(n^3 · d(n)) — same recurrence as top-down, iterated over O(n²) intervals with O(n) work per interval per divisor.
a.sp: O(n³) — the DP table stores O(n²) strings of length up to n.

w: In an interview, present the interval DP directly (Approach 2) after sketching the recursive intuition; mention the top-down version only if asked about alternatives. Common pitfalls: forgetting that encodings nest (you must recurse/DP on the block inside brackets, not just use the raw block); using the wrong periodicity test (the (t+t) trick or KMP failure function are the clean ways); skipping the strict-shortening comparison, which would wrongly output e.g. 3[a] for "aaa"; and off-by-one errors on split points. Edge cases: single characters, strings with no repeats, full-string repetitions like "aaaaaaaaaa", and mixed cases like "abbbabbbcabbbabbbc" → 2[abbbabbbc]. Likely follow-ups: count the number of distinct shortest encodings, handle multi-digit k correctly (it already works since we compare lengths numerically), or extend to allow k=1 removals.
